dependents.marginalValueRemaining: A positive commitment window you can act on where a push cannot reach you: D9 quiet hours, a muted phone, a meeting, or the Linux/Windows machines D4's own note admits have no native popup backend. It is also the only signal that survives a delivery failure, because silence from D4 is indistinguishable from 'nothing happened' and 'the notifier is broken', whereas an explicit 'clear for 40 minutes' is falsifiable. That is failure-mode insurance, not a second copy of the walk-away promise.

One clock time you can write on a calendar or hand to someone else, which supports pre-committing to a 20-minute errand before leaving rather than reacting after a ping. It also stays honest without C2 while D5 does not, so it can carry Release 1 alone. Both of those are sequencing and packaging value; once H2 delivers D4 off the desk, nobody needs to remember 3:40 because 3:40 will call them.

rationale: The unit of value is 'you can stop watching', and this board charges for it four times. D4 (shipped) is the mechanism; H2 is its off-desk delivery leg and a co-primary rather than a dependent, since without H2 the whole cluster silently assumes a user sitting at the laptop. Once the pair works, being reachable strictly dominates being told you are free: a reachable user needs no all-clear and no return time, because the interrupt finds them. Worse, the three signals are one computation in three units. D3 (shipped) computes a per-turn ETA; D6 is the minimum over those ETAs; D5 is that same minimum restated as a duration with a C2 truthfulness gate bolted on. Scoring D4 at 80, D5 at 82 and D6 at 76 books roughly 240 points of impact against one behaviour change. D7 is deliberately NOT listed here: push notification is per-event and unranked, so a ranked list is what you face after any absence, which is a different moment and a different artifact (see the D7 cluster).

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: Net of the ordering, B7 is B3's per-row 'what it is waiting for' text plus an answer-top-to-bottom interaction. The genuine residue is the interaction: a single pass that clears N gates without leaving the surface, which a sorted list does not give you. Its own note concedes the information is already on screen and all the cost is interface, so what remains is a form, not a signal.

The raw wait duration as evidence rather than as a sort key: '4 sessions blocked 40+ minutes today' is the number F3 needs to make the case for delegating. As triage it is fully absorbed, because time-blocked is precisely the key an attention sort already orders by, and it is shipped as exactly that headline number.

Only the transitions that resolved while you were gone and no longer appear in current state: a session that blocked and was auto-continued, a task that failed then passed, an error that scrolled away. Everything else in its own example ('three finished, one needs you, one stuck') is D7 ordering over E2, C2 and B1 flags, computable from the live board with no H1 at all. So D10's honest scope is a change log, not a digest, and it is the only part of it that justifies the history store.

rationale: The unit of value is one ranked attention queue: the user stops triaging by whatever they saw first. D7 already exists as calm mode's attention sort and needs only to become the default across both display modes. B7, B6 and D10 are each that same ranked list re-rendered for a narrower audience: B7 filters it to gates, B6 supplies its sort key, D10 renders it at the moment of return. Three of the four are scored as though each independently fixes 'I deal with the thing I see', which the board records as one failure. Cheapest correct read: ship D7 as the default sort, treat B6 as done, treat B7 as a UI affordance over B3, and cut D10 back to the diff-since-you-left.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: Nothing additive. C2's own needs list names 'a test re-run loop' and 'repeated identical tool calls' as its detection signals, which is C5's entire definition, so C5's finding set is a proper subset of C2's. Its independent worth is substitution, not addition: build 40 instead of 60, shippable inside one release, and it catches the single most expensive failure mode (a 5h window burned on a loop). Treat these as one line item at two ambition levels and pick one; building C5 then C2 pays the detection cost twice, and scoring both books 172 impact for one capability.

rationale: One unit of value: a wedged agent stops looking like a working agent, which is what makes walking away safe. C2 is the general form, C5 is explicitly described in its own note as 'the narrow, shippable slice of C2'. This is the cleanest either/or on the board rather than a pair. Note the knock-on: D5's honesty gate points at C2, and C5 satisfies that gate for exactly the loop-shaped stalls, which is a further reason to choose one and route the dependency at it rather than keeping both alive.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: The exact percentage and the reset clock, for a user who wants to reason instead of obeying a light: 'red, but it resets in 11 minutes, so I will wait rather than switch model'. That is real and small. A1 remains a mandatory input to A9, A2, A5, A7 and E7, so the penalty is against counting it as a user-facing feature, not against building it. Its own note already says to ship it as plumbing and never alone; at access 12 it is the most commodity item here, and A9 is where its 88 impact actually gets realised.

The multi-day horizon a start/stop light cannot express: whether to begin a large job on a Thursday at all. A9 can only encode that by becoming time-scoped, at which point it has absorbed A2. What survives independently is the weekly reset date as a planning fact.

Time-to-wall as a quantity rather than a verdict, which is what you scope the next prompt against ('22 minutes left, so ask for the small refactor') and what E7 triggers on. A9 collapses it to green/amber/red and loses the number. This is the largest surviving residue in the cluster, and the reason A5 rather than A1 is the item that earns DEC-1.

The demand side of the same comparison: A9 knows the ceiling but not the size of the job you are about to start. That is a genuine gap, and also the half nobody computes well; it needs H1 plus shape-matching against past sessions and stays speculative even then. Once A9 exists, A6 is a refinement of A9's threshold, not a separate decision.

Decoration once a projection exists. Its own note concedes a rate with no ceiling supports no decision, and the ceiling arriving is exactly what A5 and A9 do with it. What is left is the shape of the rate over time, which is diagnostic colour on a row rather than a decision.

rationale: One unit of value: permission to begin, or a reason to stop before the wall force-pauses you. The Usage column scores nine items and most of them claim that same outcome. A9's own needs line settles the direction: 'Composes A1, A2 and A5. No source beyond A1', so A9 is a strict superset of three items each scored as if it were the sole route (88 + 70 + 84 + 74 + 58 + 24 = 398 impact for one glance). A9 is the value carrier because it is the item that makes the decision; the others are its inputs, its unit conversions, or its refinements. Build A1 as the input the board already says it is, publish A5's number alongside A9's light so the residue is not lost, and hold A2, A6 and G1 back.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: Only the case where the whole account is capped, not just one model: every model at the ceiling, or a single-model harness. Then a fresh vendor is the only hatch left. Everything else about it is A1 replicated per vendor plus a comparison, at build 70 with per-vendor auth, and the user still pays to restate the task in another harness. Its own re-score to access 50 concedes each vendor already shows its own usage.

Continuity of context, which no hatch provides. A3 and A4 keep a machine working; E7 keeps the work coherent across the break. It also automates a ritual the board records the user already performing by hand, which is the highest-confidence demand signal here. Genuinely distinct value, listed only to show the escape-hatch overlap was checked and does not apply.

rationale: The escape-hatch value saturates after the first hatch that works. One situation (the wall is coming) is met by five separately scored remedies: switch model (A3), switch harness (A4), do not start (A9), stop a session (A7), hand off (E7). A user needs one cheap hatch, and A3 is the cheapest by a wide margin, one keystroke against A4's cross-vendor integration, with the per-model fields sitting in the very same payload A1 already requires. Sequencing makes it starker: if DEC-1 resolves only for Claude, A4 is unreachable anyway, so its 79 is impact that cannot be collected in the release that needs it.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: Instantaneous rate catches a session that has just started burning hard, before cumulative share moves enough to rank it, and it needs no quota source at all so it can ship in Release 1 while DEC-1 is unresolved. Beyond that it answers the identical question with a weaker denominator; its own note calls it 'the version of A7 that needs no quota', which is a substitute, not an addition.

Model identity is orthogonal to volume: Opus on a trivial task is worth catching at 10% quota, when nothing is eating the pool and A7 has nothing to flag. It is also the control surface A3 needs, since knowing the Opus limit is near is useless without knowing which sessions spend it. Mostly survives; the overlap is confined to the one case where the Opus-heavy session is also the top consumer.

rationale: One unit of value: turn 'I am at 80%' into a target you can kill. A7 ranks sessions by share of the pool, A10 ranks them by current output rate, and for the question actually being asked ('which one do I stop') those rankings mostly agree, because forward consumption is what a kill recovers. Two items, 66 + 62 impact, one decision. Ship A10 as the Release 1 stand-in and then fold it into A7 as a column rather than carrying both as features.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: As an independent capability, none: B4 cannot answer a prompt it has not rendered, so B3 is B4's first screen. Both are scored 78 for the same avoided trip. What survives is that B3 is shippable today with no DEC-2 write path, over data Cargento already parses and throws away, and that reading the question is sometimes enough on its own (you learn it is asking to force-push and decide to go and look properly).

Reaching sessions that are not at a gate: clicking into a working session to read its output, or into a stuck one C2 flagged. B4 only ever covers prompt-answering, so B5 keeps navigation for every other reason to visit a session. It is also the fallback when the write path does not exist for a given harness, which is most of them.

The answer landing in Spacedock's own record so the first officer advances entity state, which a generic write into a terminal does not do. That is workflow bookkeeping rather than unblocking, and it is the seam where Cargento joins Spacedock's flow instead of sitting beside it. Largely survives; the overlap is only the keystrokes.

rationale: One unit of value: dispose of a gate without the trip to the tab. B3 (78), B4 (78), B5 (64) and B7 (75) are four scorings of that single trip, and B4 contains all of B3 and all of B5 by construction. Listing B4 as primary is a statement about containment, not about build order: the board's own verdict, arrived at three independent ways, is that B4 is convenience at build 92 and DEC-2's cost, so the right move is to ship the residues (B3 now, B5 later) and let the primary stay unbuilt. What must not happen is scoring the residues at full value while B4 also sits on the board at 78.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: A read-only roll-up of stated goals for the user's own recall, with no drift decision attached. Its own note admits it is 'the same shape as C3' and argues for the Spacedock on-ramp rather than for a feature. Once C3 compares intent against behaviour, displaying the intent alone is a panel, not a signal.

Drift that stays inside the declared scope: the plan named three tasks, the diff did one, and nothing ever left the rails. C3 cannot see that. The residue is real and expensive, needing semantic judgement, so a local model or a third promise amendment on top of DEC-1 and DEC-2.

The user-declared threshold and a place to write it down, plus the alert edge. The stage strips are shipped and orthogonal. The tripwire half overlaps C3's comparison directly, and its delivery half is D4's; what is uniquely C1's is letting the user name the line rather than having the product infer it, which is also the thing that makes the signal trustworthy enough to leave on.

rationale: One unit of value: know when a session has left the path it was supposed to be on. C1's tripwire, C3, C4 and C7 all require the same missing ingredient, a declared intent to compare actual behaviour against, and all four are nearly free under Spacedock and guesswork outside it. That shared dependency is the tell: this is one comparison engine with four presentations, scored at 77 + 72 + 66 + 48. Build the comparison once against Spacedock stage and scope, then decide which presentations to expose.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: The honest catch-all for harnesses where neither a SessionEnd nor a completion classifier fires, which E3's own note says is most of the other eight. As a user-facing signal it is fully subsumed: its documented gloss ('either it finished and nobody read it, or it is waiting on a reply that never came') is a confession that it is E2 and E3 unseparated, and E2's note says splitting them is the entire value. Being shipped is why the penalty is a scoring correction rather than a build decision.

Almost all of it. Finished-and-unread is a reward you collect and died-rather-than-finished is a chore you restart; the remedies are opposite, so these are siblings rather than duplicates. Listed to record that the overlap was checked: they share only the detector that decides why a session went quiet, so build one classifier with two outputs and count the value once.

rationale: One unit of value: a quiet session gets classified instead of all quiet sessions looking alike. E1 (shipped, 54), E2 (73) and E3 (77) are three scorings of one classifier over the same idle event, and E1 is exactly the undifferentiated version the other two exist to replace. E3 is primary because waiting on something that is never coming back is the costlier error, and because SessionEnd already arrives for Claude. Do not book E1's 54 alongside them.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: The review-stalled case a dirty-tree check cannot see: work committed and pushed, tree clean, branch or PR sitting untouched. That is a different loss (stalled in review) from E4's (never saved), and it needs a remote call E4 does not. It also needs everything E4 needs first, per its own note, so it can never ship earlier or cheaper.

rationale: One unit of value: agent work does not evaporate in a directory nobody went back to. E4 and E5 both reach into a user's repository for git state, which E4's note correctly identifies as a third promise amendment more invasive than fetching a quota number, and they pay that cost for the same outcome. E5 is E4 plus a remote lookup, so the amendment buys both or neither. Build E4, and add E5 as a second query against the same access rather than as a separate item at 56.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: Machine identity and other people's sessions, which is a different buyer and arguably a different product; F4 stops at 'my cloud and my laptop'. Everything underneath it, transport, auth and the end of the local-only story, is F4's work, as its own needs line concedes.

Entirely contingent, and the contingency is worth resolving before scoring it: if Cowork writes a local artifact, F5 is just another collector and owes nothing to F4; if it does not, F5 is F4's remote-source work applied to one more vendor. Its own note files it as a feasibility question, which is the right treatment. Answer that first, then it is either cheap and independent or subsumed.

rationale: One unit of value: the board covers the sessions the user actually has, rather than only the ones on this laptop. D1 is that value for local sources and is shipped. F4 (72), F5 (55) and F7 (60) each extend it to sources that are not local, and each is scored as if it independently completes the board. It does not compound: coverage saturates the moment the user's own sources are all present, and every further source is worth roughly nothing to that user. All three also spend the same one-time cost, the end of local-only plus transport and auth, which should be paid once and attributed once.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: The unprompted noticing: you cannot promote a project you had not realised was one project, and F1 is the only item that spots the group. Shipped alone, though, it is a suggestion with no accept button, which is a nag rather than a capability, and F6 requires it anyway. Its real independent worth is being the cheap probe of whether users want the promotion at all before DEC-2 is paid for.

A different granularity of the same move: automate a repeated decision rather than a repeated project, so the target is a skill and not a workflow. That distinction survives F6 intact. What does not survive is the framing value, since once F6 has changed the user's role from operator to orchestrator, F2 is an optimisation inside the new role rather than the thing that changes it.

The artifact for a human audience: the week you can show a manager, or yourself, to authorise the delegation. That is persuasion, not capability, and its own note is explicit that it exists to change behaviour. It survives as the reason someone accepts F1's proposal, and it collapses as an independent outcome, because attention data nobody acts on is G4 with better framing.

rationale: One unit of value: the user stops being the orchestrator. F1 spots the pattern, F6 acts on it, F2 does the same at skill granularity, F3 builds the case for doing any of it, and the four are scored 80 + 80 + 78 + 74 for one role change. F6 is primary because it is the only item where the role actually changes; the others are its detector, its evidence and its smaller sibling. Sequencing caveat worth keeping visible: F6 needs DEC-2 and is the most expensive item on the board, so the practical plan ships F1 alone as a demand probe, which is fine as long as F1 is not also credited with F6's 80.

dependents.marginalValueRemaining: None beyond decoration. F3's dataset (hours spent answering agents, which decisions repeat) strictly contains G4's (sessions this week, streaks), computed from the same H1 store. Its own note already files it as vanity listed for honesty. If F3 ships, G4 is a stylesheet over data that is already there; if F3 does not, G4 is a poor reason to build H1, which its needs line concedes.

rationale: Small but exact containment: two items reading the same history store to describe the same week, one with a decision attached and one without. Kept as its own line rather than folded into the F6 cluster because the primary here is the evidence layer, not the role change.

subsets: C5 subset of C2 - C2's needs list names C5's exact detection signals (repeated identical tool calls, a test re-run loop), so C5's finding set is contained in C2's. Substitute, not addition.
B3 subset of B4 - B4 must render the prompt to answer it, so B3 is literally B4's first screen; both scored 78 for the same avoided trip.
B5 subset of B4 - B5 ends the hunt across tabs, which B4 also ends and then goes further. B4's own note calls B5 its cheap half.
B7 subset of (D7 + B3) - a gate-filtered slice of the attention sort, with B3's text on each row; nothing in it is new information, and its note admits all the cost is interface.
B6 subset of D7 - time-blocked is the attention sort's key, and B6 ships as exactly that headline number on blocked rows.
D6 subset of D5 - the same minimum-over-ETAs value in a different unit; D5 is D6 restated as a duration plus a C2 honesty gate.
D6 subset of D3 (aggregated) - the minimum over per-turn ETAs Cargento already computes and already displays.
D10 subset of (D7 + E2 + E3 + C2) - 'three finished, one needs you, one stuck' is the live board grouped and sorted; only transitions that resolved while away are outside that union.
A1, A2 and A5 subset of A9 - stated outright in A9's needs: 'Composes A1, A2 and A5. No source beyond A1.'
G1 subset of A5 - the rate without a ceiling versus the rate projected against one; A5 is G1 plus the number that makes it a decision.
A6 subset of A9's question - both answer 'should I start', A6 adding a task-size estimate that needs H1 and stays speculative.
A10 subset of A7 - the same 'which one do I stop' ranking with a weaker denominator; A10's note calls itself the version of A7 that needs no quota.
E1 subset of (E2 union E3) - E1's documented gloss is E2 and E3 unseparated, and E2's note says separating them is the entire value.
E4 subset of E5 - E5 needs everything E4 needs plus a remote PR lookup, so it can never ship earlier or cheaper.
C4 subset of C3 - C4 displays the declared intent, C3 compares behaviour against it; same missing ingredient, and C4's note says it argues for the on-ramp rather than for a feature.
F1 subset of F6 - F6 requires F1 and then adds the accept button; F1 alone is the suggestion half.
F7 subset of F4 - F7's needs line is 'everything F4 needs' plus machine identity.
G4 subset of F3 - both read the same H1 store to describe the same week; F3 attaches a decision, G4 does not.
G2 subset of D1 - a count is a trivially derived summary of the list D1 already renders.
G5 subset of D1 - its own note says the shipped discovered-harnesses strip already covers most of the real need.
D2 subset of D1 - a per-row field of the one-screen view rather than a separate signal.
